chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Al-Amraki, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), said:
I asked him about a man whose hand was cut off from the elbow, 'How does he perform the ablution?' He said: 'He washes whatever remains of his upper arm.'
ai.seo_question: How does a person with a hand amputated at the elbow perform ritual ablution (wudu)?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the principle of *takhyir* (ease) in Shia jurisprudence, where the obligation of washing the arm is limited to the portion that remains attached to the body. Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS) provides a precise anatomical boundary, ruling that the upper arm (*'ud*) is washed up to the point of amputation rather than requiring the washing of the entire limb as if it were intact. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on practical applicability and the removal of undue hardship (*raf' al-haraj*) in ritual purity laws.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Al Amraky, 
(It has been narrated) from Ali son of Ja’far<sup>asws</sup>, from his brother<sup>asws</sup> Musa<sup>asws</sup> Bin Ja’far<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘
I asked himasws about a man with a hand cut off from the elbow, ‘How would he perform the Ablution (Wudhu)?’ Heasws said: ‘He should wash whatever remains from his limb’.
en.sarwar: 9. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from al-‘Amrakiy from Ali ibn Ja‘far who has said the following: “I asked my brother, Musa ibn Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam,
about a man whose hand is cut off from the elbow. How he should take Wudu’? He (the Imam) said, ‘He must wash what is left of his arm.’”
